title: A Queen Mole-Rat's Scent Helps Keep Her Colony Calm
summary:
Naked mole-rats live together in groups called colonies. Some members search for food. Others care for the young. The queen has babies. A study found that a special scent from the queen helps keep other members from fighting or reproducing, which means having young.

Gary Lewin studies how naked mole-rats use their senses. He is a scientist at the Max Delbrück Center in Berlin, Germany. He had found that these animals use scent to recognize mole-rats from other colonies. His team wanted to learn whether smells also matter within a colony.

The researchers found a chemical called isopropyl myristate that only the queens produced among the mole-rats they studied. It activated the part of the animals' brains that handles smells.

To test the chemical, the team removed a queen from her colony. They then added the chemical every day for three months. During that time, the animals did not fight or mate. Mating is part of animal reproduction. When the team stopped adding the scent, fighting began. A few weeks later, the animals began mating, and a new queen emerged.

In another experiment, the researchers separated male and female pairs from the colony. Some pairs received the queen's scent; others did not. After four weeks, none of the females exposed to the scent had mated. Five of the six females without it were pregnant.

The team also found that the chemical changed hormones in female mole-rats. Hormones are chemical signals in the body. These findings help explain how a queen's scent can affect life in a colony.
why_it_matters: The experiments help explain how a queen's scent affects both behavior and reproduction in a naked mole-rat colony.
